payload.text: Do the interaction terms help, and by how much? (whether adding feature interaction terms improves held-out AUROC on a synthetic two-class set)

payload.query: Friedman & Popescu (2008), 'Predictive learning via rule ensembles': the H-statistic for detecting and measuring feature interactions.
Lou, Caruana, Gehrke & Hooker (2013), 'Accurate intelligible models with pairwise interactions' (GA2M/FAST): a competing way to choose and add pairwise interaction terms.
Bien, Taylor & Tibshirani (2013), 'A lasso for hierarchical interactions': sparse selection of interaction terms with a penalty, the standard alternative to adding all pairwise products.
Rendle (2010), 'Factorization Machines': learns pairwise interactions implicitly, a competing method for the same task.
Tsang, Cheng & Liu (2018), 'Detecting statistical interactions from neural network weights': shows flexible models learn interactions without explicit terms.
Chen & Guestrin (2016), 'XGBoost': gradient-boosted trees, the usual tabular baseline that captures interactions through its splits.
DeLong, DeLong & Clarke-Pearson (1988): a test for comparing two correlated AUROCs measured on the same held-out set.
Dietterich (1998), 'Approximate statistical tests for comparing supervised classification learning algorithms': variance and paired testing when comparing two models.

payload.answer: Q14 What is O1's baseline arm: the same logistic regression trained on x1..x4 alone, without the x3*x4 column? Answer: yes: the same model, optimiser, epochs, and seeds, differing only in the x3*x4 input column
payload.rationale:
What this means: the baseline arm is today's train.py run with one change. featurize() leaves out row['interaction'] (the x3*x4 column), so the model sees only x1..x4. The baseline shares everything else with the arm that keeps the column: the model, optimiser, epochs, any regularisation, each pair's generator seed and training seed, the held-out fifth, and eval.py.

Why:
(1) A settled decision binds this. In Q7 the owner rejected objection 2, and the reason on record is that 'the claim stays limited to explicit terms against the same model without them'. In Q4 the owner parked O5, the objective that covered tree ensembles and MLPs. So the baseline can't be another model class, or a separately tuned model. This answer just spells out Q7's 'the same model without them'.
(2) Q8 (concern K2, tied to O1) asks for a confidence interval over seeds and a paired test. POSITION.md defines O1's answer as the paired AUROC difference '(with interaction terms minus without)', with a DeLong or paired-bootstrap test on each split. Those tests only work if both arms are scored on the same held-out rows, so each pair must share its generator seed. Sharing the training seed too keeps initialisation and shuffling noise out of the difference. If the arms differed in anything besides the column, the gap couldn't be put down to the column.
(3) The optimiser and epochs are fixed and shared, so neither arm is tuned at all. That means nothing is tuned on the held-out fifth, in line with Q9.
(4) The evidence says featurize() always appends the column. No run without it exists yet, so O1 can't be answered until one does. The intake asks whether 'the interaction terms' help, meaning the ones the code already adds, so the arm with the term stays as it runs today.

The line. This is not a `data` decision: the rows generate.py draws, the held-out split, and what leaves the machine all stay the same. One arm's model just doesn't get one derived column, and that comparison is what O1 (opened by the owner in Q1) asks about. It is not an `objective` decision either, as long as three conditions hold: the switch in train.py is opt-in, today's with-term run stays the default, and baseline runs write their summaries to their own paths, never over the summary O2's measure reads. Then O2's metric, target, split, and command don't change. Nothing is deleted, pushed, or spent. To reverse this: `wayline grill answer Q14 ... --revise`.

Not decided here: how many seeds (Q15); whether the treatment arm should add more terms than x3*x4 (x1..x4 alone stays the baseline either way); the null control (O4).

Why not more confident: src/toy/train.py is not among the paths I may open, so I haven't checked the grill's description of the model as logistic regression. The answer says 'the same model', so it holds whatever train.py fits. If the work finds either arm hasn't converged at the shared number of epochs, this answer should be revisited.

payload.answer: Q15 How many paired generator and training seeds does each arm run? Answer: 20 paired seeds per arm and per sweep point
payload.rationale:
What this means: every comparison the work runs for O1, and every point of O4's sweep, uses 20 replicates. Replicate i gets its own generator seed and its own training seed. The generator seed is a fresh draw from generate.py, scored on that draw's last fifth, which is the held-out rule the intake states. There is one training seed per generator seed, not every combination of the two. Both arms of replicate i (with and without the x3*x4 column) share both seeds, as Q14 settled. So one comparison is 40 train.py runs. The 20 seeds are fixed before any result is read, and every one is reported. No seed is dropped or added because of how a result came out.

Why:
(1) Settled decisions already require paired replicates; this answer only sets how many. In Q8 the owner accepted objection 3 (K2, tied to O1). The reason on record is that 'by how much needs a confidence interval over seeds and a paired test'. The objection's complaint is 'one seeded stream and one held-out fifth', so the generator seed must vary, not just the training seed. Q14 pairs the arms on both seeds. In Q3 the owner opened O4, which is where 'per sweep point' applies.
(2) 20 is enough for what K2 asks. Take SD to be how much the per-seed AUROC difference varies from seed to seed. With 20 seeds, the 95% confidence interval on the mean difference is ±t(19)·SD/√20 ≈ ±0.47·SD. So a one-point gap (0.01) can be told apart from zero whenever SD is under about 0.02.
  - An illustration, not something I measured: a single AUROC near 0.8 on 2,000 balanced held-out rows has a standard error of about 0.01 (Hanley–McNeil). Scoring both arms on the same rows keeps the error of their difference at about that level or below.
  - So 20 seeds resolve 'a point or two' unless each held-out fifth is only a few hundred rows.
  - 20 pairs also leave the paired test room to work. An exact signed-rank test can reach p ≈ 2×10⁻⁶ with 20 pairs. With the 5 seeds common in ML papers, its smallest two-sided p is 0.0625, so it could never reject at 0.05.
(3) It is cheap. At the 4.4 s per run in the grill's evidence, one comparison takes about 3 minutes. A 20-point O4 grid takes about an hour at the size that was timed, and longer where the sweep enlarges the training set. That fits POSITION.md's compute note: 'a few dozen seeded replicates of two models, plus a sweep over interaction strength, should fit in an overnight run on one GPU'. INTAKE.md states no GPU or wall-clock budget, so none is exceeded or raised.
(4) Why not 30 or 50? The interval only narrows as 1/√n. 50 seeds take it from ±0.47·SD to ±0.28·SD but cost 2.5 times the runs, and that multiplier applies across O4's whole grid, whose size isn't set yet. No record asks for finer resolution than K2's 'a point or two', so the records don't argue against the recommendation.

The line. This is not a `data` decision. generate.py, its held-out rule (the last fifth of each draw, used only for evaluation), and what leaves the machine all stay as they are. Q8 already made the work vary the seeded stream; this answer only sets the count. It is not an `objective` decision either, as long as the condition Q14 set holds: every replicate writes its summary to its own path, never over the summary O2's measure reads, and never into owner/. O2 stays the single run its command measures; it is not redefined as a mean over seeds. Nothing is deleted, pushed, or spent. To reverse this: `wayline grill answer Q15 ... --revise`.

When to revisit: raise the count in two cases.
  - The first 20 seeds show an SD above about 0.02, so the interval can't separate a one-point gain from zero.
  - At O4's zero-strength and smallest-sample points, the interval is too wide to bound the overfitting cost that objection 5 (K4) asks about.
Decide this on the interval's width, never on whether a result came out significant, and report every seed run.

Not decided here:
  - which seed values to use (seeds 1–20 would let seed 1's with-term run be checked against owner/sample-summary.json);
  - whether every sweep point reuses the same seed list;
  - O4's grid;
  - the analysis (a paired t-test or signed-rank test across seeds, and DeLong per split).

Why not more confident:
  - The SD that decides whether 20 is enough is unknown until the first batch runs.
  - src/toy/*.py and owner/sample-summary.json are not among the paths I may open, so I haven't checked the row count or the 4.4 s figure.
  - Runs are so cheap that an owner could reasonably prefer 30 or 50.

findings.text: A6's trigger is E1's population ceiling on D2. O2, though, is one finite-sample run on D5's held-out fifth, and that run can land above the ceiling by chance, so when bayes_auroc sits just under 0.82, E1 cannot confirm 'no model can meet O2 … C7 is wrong by construction'. E5 step 1 scores the default run either way, so the spec's own rules let A6 be confirmed and C7 supported at the same time.

A7 compares the goal run with E2's 20-seed mean_auroc_with, but E2 runs the pinned configs/arms.json, which Methods deliberately keeps clear of E5's changes. Once E5 keeps a change, the goal run is a different model and E2 no longer measures the 'model's expected held-out AUROC' that A7 needs. That is exactly the selection-over-reads case (K3) A7 exists to guard, and E2 also cannot supply A7's other trigger, the goal run, which only E5 produces.

E4 supports C6 on the point estimate gain_shrink <= 0.005, and the spec defines no gain_shrink_hi. So the noisy smallest-size point, which the Risks expect to be wide, can 'support' C6 while its CI reaches well above 0.005, whereas C4 needs its whole CI inside the margin. The test also passes vacuously when the gain is near zero at every size: under A1, E4 adopts no absolute-weight fallback (unlike E3), and its m = 1 point reuses E2's default runs, which are then null.

C1 says the x3·x4 term is worth more than 0.005 AUROC over the best additive model. But additive_gap is the full oracle's AUROC minus the additive LR's, so it credits x3·x4 with any other non-additive structure in the label, and the Risks anticipate rule-based or latent-noise labels. Fitting the same LR with x3·x4 added, against B4 on the same D2 halves, would isolate the term.

A1 fires on a zero weight or on additive_gap <= 0.005, and says E3's strength axis then switches to absolute weights. E3 switches only 'If E1 finds the default weight is zero', so with a small nonzero weight the two disagree on what C5's multipliers are.

A2 covers C3 failing only through the CI, so paired_gain_lo > 0 with signed_rank_p >= 0.05 leaves C3 unsupported with no anti-claim and no stated reading. A4 likewise covers only the lower side of C4's margin, not a CI that reaches above +0.01 at m = 0.

E4 can confirm that the gain falls as training rows grow, but nothing in E4 measures A5's 'train.py's model is learning x3·x4 without the column'. If configs/arms.json records a linear model, as C6 assumes, that explanation is impossible; comparing the without arm's AUROC at 4·n0 with B4's additive reference would test it.

C8 covers all five D6 works, yet E6 supports it at resolved_refs >= 4, so one work may go unread. C8's second sentence, what each work does instead, is held in no placement.json field and checked by no metric.

measures_paired_gain drops C8's 'read against a known Bayes ceiling', so A9 can declare 'C8 is wrong' on a work that measures the gain against a no-interaction control without a ceiling, which C8 as worded does not rule out. Support is sound, because the flag is broader than C8's definition; only A9's refutation overreaches.

C7 is about train.py's default with-term run, but E5's candidates include input-column sets drawn from x1..x4 and their six pairwise products, which may drop x3·x4. E5's success criterion does not check that the kept default still carries the term.

payload.rationale:
What this means: the spec as it stands at commit 2dc923e571bb is confirmed, and the planner may now cut the tickets from it. Ticket 1 is blocking: all, so until it is answered no other ticket launches.

Why:
(1) The recommended answer is confirm, and no record argues against it. The ticket's evidence says the spec passed its structural checks and the verifier's verdict, both at that exact commit. DECISIONS.md has nothing open ("Nothing is open"), so no design question is left that the spec would have to wait for. No settled decision conflicts with confirming.
(2) The settled decisions already fix what the spec has to carry, and they bind every ticket whatever the spec's wording:
  - O1 (Q1): the paired difference in held-out AUROC, with the x3*x4 column versus without it. Same model, optimiser, epochs, and seeds (Q14). 20 paired generator-and-training seeds (Q15). A confidence interval and a paired test (K2, Q8). The claims placed against real prior work (K7, Q13).
  - O2 (Q5): held-out AUROC of at least 0.82, measured by `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m toy.eval --split held_out`. Any tuning uses a validation split cut from the training rows (K3, Q9).
  - O3 (Q2): what generate.py plants, and its Bayes-optimal AUROC as the ceiling (K5, Q11).
  - O4 (Q3): the null control, and the sweeps over interaction strength and sample size (K1, K4, K6; Q6, Q10, Q12).
  - O5 is parked (Q4) and objective 2 was rejected (Q7), so there is no tree-ensemble or MLP arm.
  A ticket that contradicts these is wrong whatever the spec says. What confirming can't rule out is something left out, which is why the morning check below lists what to look for.
(3) Leaving it open costs the night. You asked for the project to 'run on its own overnight once it is set up' (INTAKE.md, constraints), which is why autonomy is autonomous. Because the ticket is blocking: all, waiting until morning would stop the whole run. Confirming is cheap to take back: the planner can cut the tickets again from a revised spec. Overnight runs delete or overwrite nothing, because Q14 and Q15 require every replicate to write its summary to its own path. At worst some cheap runs get re-run (the grill's evidence puts one at about 4.4 s).

The line. Confirming deletes nothing, pushes nothing, spends nothing, and raises no budget (INTAKE.md states no GPU or wall-clock budget). It is not an `objective`, `data`, or `ladder` decision:
  - it adds, reframes, or reopens no objective;
  - O2's metric, target, split, and command stay as OBJECTIVES.md records them;
  - the data stays as INTAKE.md states it: generate.py's seeded rows, with the last fifth held out for evaluation only.
The ticket itself is marked human-only: no. One limit: if the spec says anything that would change O2's measure, the data, or the stopping rule, or reopen O5, this answer does not confirm that part. That part stays yours. Nothing in the records suggests the spec does any of these.

What I could not check. research/SPEC.md is not among the paths this session may open, so I have not read its claims myself. This confirmation rests on the structural checks, the verdict, and the settled decisions above, not on my own reading of the spec. That is the main reason my confidence is not higher.

What to look for in the morning: read SPEC.md against the list in (2), and revise if:
  - an open objective (O1–O4) or an open concern (K1–K7) has no claim;
  - anything may be tuned on the held-out fifth;
  - it compares against another model class, which Q7 ruled out;
  - the seed count or the baseline differs from Q15 or Q14.

To reverse: answer ticket 1 again as `revise: <what to change>` with `wayline answer 1 "revise: ..." --project .`, or from the dashboard's decisions view. The planner then cuts the tickets again from the revised spec.
